title: How Career Services Can Run Better Employer Information Sessions
summary: Learn how career services teams can run more effective employer information sessions by choosing the right formats, preparing recruiters, encouraging meaningful student interactions, and turning session participation into applications and recruiting opportunities.
body_markdown:
## How can career centers improve employer information sessions?


Career centers can improve employer information sessions by choosing formats based on recruiting goals, preparing employers to share practical insights, making sessions interactive, and defining clear next steps for students. Success should be measured by meaningful employer interactions and recruiting actions, not attendance alone.


If your career center regularly hosts employer information sessions, you know that getting students to attend doesn't necessarily mean they're getting much out of the experience.


Too often, students sit through company presentations filled with information they could have found online, ask a few questions, and leave without a clear next step.


Employers, meanwhile, may struggle to connect with students who are genuinely interested in their opportunities.


The difference often comes down to how the session is designed, what employers are asked to share, and how those interactions translate into recruiting opportunities.


This guide explains how career services teams can make employer information sessions more relevant, interactive, and valuable for both students and recruiters.


## How Should Career Centers Choose the Right Employer Information Session Format?


Choose the format based on what the employer wants students to do after attending. A company introducing unfamiliar career opportunities needs a different session from one recruiting for an internship with an approaching deadline. Career services teams should establish that objective first, then decide how much time to allocate to[employer presentations](https://www.hiration.com/blog/career-center-employer-partnership-strategy-higher-ed/) , recruiter questions, and individual conversations.


The[University of Washington Information School](https://ischool.uw.edu/partners/employers/host-information-session) makes a useful distinction between structured information sessions and more conversational virtual hangouts.


Its information sessions typically include company and hiring information followed by Q&A, while hangouts emphasize informal student-employer dialogue.


Career centers can use a similar distinction when choosing among three formats.


Session format Best suited for What students should gain


Employer presentation with Q&A Introducing an unfamiliar company, team, or internship program Clarity about opportunities, requirements, and the recruiting process


Recruiter-led Q&A Employers with advertised vacancies or approaching application deadlines Answers about selection criteria, hiring timelines, and application expectations


Small-group recruiter discussions Employers seeking more substantial conversations with prospective applicants Direct access to recruiters or employees working in relevant roles


**Do not automatically choose virtual sessions because they're easier to schedule.**


According to[Handshake's 2025 Campus to Career report](https://joinhandshake.com/blog/employers/campus-recruiting-strategies-campus-career-report-key-findings/) , 69% of surveyed students said connecting with employers was easier at in-person events, while 62% found virtual events more convenient.


These are[general career-event](https://www.hiration.com/blog/career-center-events-strategy-higher-ed/) preferences, not measured information-session outcomes. Still, they suggest a useful distinction:


- **Choose in-person sessions** when the central value is direct conversation with employees and recruiters.
- **Choose virtual sessions** when students need access to geographically distant employers or speakers across locations.
- **Use small-group formats** when the employer wants detailed conversations rather than broad company exposure.


Timing should also reflect the recruiting objective.


[UC Berkeley Career Engagement](https://career.berkeley.edu/employers/build-your-campus-brand/information-sessions/) recommends scheduling employer information sessions during application periods or[following career fairs](https://www.hiration.com/blog/college-career-fairs-guide/) .


For example, a career center could schedule a recruiter Q&A shortly before an internship application deadline. Students would then have time to act on what they learn rather than waiting several weeks before applications open.


The principle is simple: choose the session format and timing together, based on the recruiting action you want to support.


Choosing the right employer information session format


## How Can Career Services Prepare Employers to Deliver a Valuable Session?


Send employers a content brief that specifies what students need to learn, not just logistical instructions. Ask recruiters to explain the work behind advertised positions, the evidence they look for in applications, and the hiring decisions students should prepare for. This gives employers a clearer presentation objective and reduces time spent repeating information already available online.


**What should the employer briefing contain?**


Instead of requesting a standard company presentation, give employers five specific content requirements.


**1. Explain the actual work.**


Ask the employer to demonstrate a task, project, or decision that an entry-level employee encounters.


For example, rather than describing an analyst internship as "cross-functional and fast-paced," a recruiter could show how interns investigate a business problem, organize findings, and present recommendations.


**2. Distinguish required qualifications from preferred experience.**


Ask recruiters to explain[which skills are essential](https://www.hiration.com/blog/recruiter-expectations-career-center-guide-higher-ed/) , which can be learned after hiring, and what kinds of coursework or student experiences may demonstrate relevant ability.


This is particularly useful when students assume that every qualification listed in a posting is mandatory.


**3. Explain how applications are evaluated.**


Encourage employers to discuss what strong candidates demonstrate during resume screening, interviews, and assessments.


For example, a recruiter could explain what distinguishes a strong problem-solving example from a vague claim of having analytical skills.


**4. Bring someone who knows the job.**


Request a recent graduate, early-career employee, or hiring manager alongside the recruiter.


They should explain responsibilities, challenges, and the transition from college to work, not repeat the organization's values.


**5. Make the recruiting process transparent.**


Ask employers to clarify application deadlines,[ai screening opt outs](https://www.hiration.com/blog/ai-screening-opt-outs-career-center-guide-higher-ed/) , interview stages, expected timelines, work-location requirements, and relevant eligibility restrictions.


Students should not need a separate appointment simply to understand how to pursue an opportunity discussed during the event.


These recommendations align with[Duke University's Fuqua School of Business](https://www.fuqua.duke.edu/employers/campus-virtual-recruiting-options/employer-presentation) , which advises employers to share information students cannot readily find online, discuss real business cases, include alumni, and provide clear recruiting next steps.


**One useful addition: request two questions before approving the presentation.**


Ask the employer:


- What is one thing students commonly misunderstand about applying to your organization?
- What can students learn from your representatives that they cannot learn from your careers website?


Use the answers to shape the session description and guide the presentation.


This helps career services teams identify whether the employer is offering useful career information or primarily delivering a company advertisement.


## How Can Career Centers Make Employer Information Sessions More Interactive?


Limit formal presentations and reserve meaningful time for recruiter-student discussion. Interaction should help students understand the work, evaluate their fit, and clarify application requirements. Career services staff can make this more productive by collecting questions beforehand, moderating discussions, and giving students opportunities to speak with representatives whose roles match their interests.


[Duke Fuqua](https://www.fuqua.duke.edu/employers/campus-virtual-recruiting-options/employer-presentation) surveyed hundreds of students about effective employer presentations and used that feedback to develop practical recommendations.


Its suggested in-person structure includes approximately 20 minutes of formal presentation followed by 20-25 minutes of Q&A or networking.


For virtual sessions, it recommends themed breakout rooms organized around functions, locations, or student questions.


One particularly useful recommendation is to make presentations interactive without putting individual students on the spot.


Career centers can implement that through three techniques:


**Use questions collected before the session.**


Invite registered students to submit one question about the role, recruiting process, or organization.


The career services moderator can group similar questions and prioritize those that offer information beyond the employer's website.


**Replace generic presentations with work examples.**


Ask employers to use a realistic scenario from an entry-level role.


For instance, a marketing employer could demonstrate how a team evaluates campaign performance. Students could then ask what analytical skills candidates need and how those skills are assessed during recruitment.


**Organize conversations by role or function.**


When several employer representatives attend, divide discussions into clearly identified groups, such as engineering, operations, or business analytics.


Students can then speak with someone whose experience matches their interests rather than competing for attention in a general networking queue.


### Sample agenda: 30-minute internship recruiting briefing


This shorter format works when an employer has active opportunities and students mainly need clarification before applying.


Time Activity


0–3 minutes Career services introduces the session objective and available roles


3–10 minutes Recruiter explains internship responsibilities, eligibility, and hiring timeline


10–17 minutes Employee shares a real project and the skills used


17–25 minutes Moderated Q&A using student-submitted questions


25–30 minutes Application instructions, deadlines, and follow-up options


**Best practice:** Send students the relevant job descriptions before the session so that the limited discussion time focuses on questions the postings do not answer.


### Sample agenda: 60-minute interactive employer session


Use this format when students need to understand several functions or have meaningful conversations with employer representatives.


Time Activity


0–5 minutes Welcome, session objective, and introduction of representatives


5–15 minutes Employer overview focused on current roles and recruiting opportunities


15–25 minutes Employee-led demonstration of a real work example


25–45 minutes Small-group recruiter discussions organized by role or function


45–55 minutes Moderated Q&A addressing common recruiting questions


55–60 minutes Application guidance, deadlines, and available follow-up opportunities


These are suggested formats, not published university agendas. They adapt the interaction-focused practices recommended by Duke Fuqua and the University of Washington.


For virtual sessions, use named breakout rooms rather than assigning students randomly. If students cannot reach every recruiter, provide a shared question-submission channel and a clear alternative for follow-up.

## How Can Career Services Turn Employer Information Sessions Into Recruiting Opportunities?


End every recruiting-focused session with a defined next step for interested students and an agreed follow-up responsibility for the employer. This might involve submitting an application, registering for recruiter office hours, or requesting a role-specific conversation. Career centers should then measure whether students take those actions, rather than treating attendance as the primary outcome.


**Establish a clear follow-up process.**


A practical approach is to divide responsibilities between the employer and career center.


**Immediately after the session:**


- The career center shares relevant application links, deadlines, and presentation resources.
- The employer provides a contact or approved process for follow-up questions.
- Interested students receive instructions for the next recruiting step, including any available recruiter conversations.


**Within the next 48 hours:**


- The employer follows up with students who requested further contact, where appropriate and permitted.
- Career services sends attendees a short reminder of the application deadline and available support.
- Students who need help translating their experiences into job-specific evidence can be directed to career advising resources.


The timing above is a recommended workflow, not a research-established requirement.


A useful employer example comes from National Grid, whose early-careers team uses Handshake Events to track student interactions.


According to[Handshake's account of National Grid's event recruiting process](https://joinhandshake.com/blog/employers/turn-candidates-into-hires-with-handshake-events/) , nearly 50% of event check-ins in the reported period received a follow-up message.


The company also analyzes attendee characteristics and post-event applications to understand which recruiting activities lead to further engagement.


This example covers recruiting events generally, rather than employer information sessions specifically, but illustrates the importance of connecting event participation with subsequent recruiting activity.


**What should career centers measure beyond attendance?**


Start with four measures:


Metric What it reveals


Attendance rate Actual attendees divided by registered students


Post-session action rate Attendees who complete a defined next step, such as registering for recruiter office hours


Application conversion rate Attendees who submit a relevant application divided by total attendees, where employer data is available


Recruiting progression Attendees who receive subsequent recruiter conversations, screening invitations, or interviews


Career centers can request aggregate application and interview figures from participating employers when individual-level reporting is unavailable or inappropriate.


For a recruiting-focused session, review early actions after approximately one week and application progression after the relevant deadline. These review points should reflect the employer's actual hiring schedule.


Do not assume an application resulted solely from attending the event. Students may have encountered the employer through several channels.


The stronger evaluation question is whether the session helped students make informed recruiting decisions and whether the employer gained meaningful contact with relevant candidates.


Finally, use employer feedback to improve the next session. Ask which student questions were most useful, whether the attendees matched the intended recruiting audience, and what information would have helped students prepare better.


## Wrapping Up


A successful employer information session shouldn't end when the recruiter leaves. Students should walk away knowing which opportunities fit their interests, what employers expect, and how to take the next step.

## Employer Information Sessions — FAQs


What makes an employer information session effective?


An effective session helps students understand actual roles, hiring expectations, and application requirements while providing meaningful interaction with employer representatives.


How should career centers choose the right session format?


Choose in-person, virtual, or small-group formats based on recruiting goals, student access, and the level of interaction employers want.


What should employers include in information sessions?


Employers should explain actual job responsibilities, essential qualifications, application evaluation, recruiting timelines, and insights students cannot easily find online.


How can career centers make employer sessions interactive?


Limit presentations, collect student questions beforehand, use real work examples, and organize role-specific discussions or breakout rooms.


How long should an employer information session last?


A 30-minute briefing can work for active recruiting opportunities, while a 60-minute session allows more time for interactive discussions and networking.


How should career centers follow up after a session?


Share application links, deadlines, and resources with students, while employers provide clear routes for further questions or recruiter conversations.


How should career centers measure session success?


Look beyond attendance to student follow-up actions, applications, recruiter interactions, and progression toward interviews where data is available.
